974.title: Abuse and the churches
974.hook: abuse and its cover-up in churches of more than one tradition have caused deep harm; survivors deserve belief and justice
974.howItsDone: Churches across traditions have adopted safeguarding policies, background checks for anyone working with children, and named people to whom abuse can be reported, alongside reporting to the police. Some hold services of lament and apology with survivors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rwanda, and clothes on the benches of a memorial church. Your line: never again, truly.

Before anything else: today's lesson is about abuse in churches. If it touches your own story, you can stop here, and nothing is lost. A grown man sits in a church office across from an official. Slowly, he tells what a trusted leader did to him when he was a boy. The official listens, nods, writes something down, and thanks him for coming. Then nothing happens. The leader is quietly moved somewhere else, where nobody knows. Today, a wound inside the churches, and what the Bible says to those who caused it.

Journalists, courts, survivors and church inquiries have uncovered the abuse of children and vulnerable adults by priests, pastors, youth leaders and volunteers, in Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox, Protestant and evangelical churches. This is not one church's story. Survivors describe a second harm: the cover-up. Leaders who moved abusers to new places. Families pressed to keep quiet for the sake of the church's name. Children who told and weren't believed. The Bible is not quiet about this. Jesus sets a child among his disciples and says, in the King James Bible: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea." In King James English, to offend is to make someone stumble. The prophet Ezekiel had turned on leaders who feed themselves instead of the flock: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?" And Jesus warns that hiding doesn't last: "For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest." Forgiveness has sometimes been used as a weapon here, survivors pushed to forgive and stay silent. But survivors and their advocates insist forgiving is not hiding, and doesn't replace justice. Churches in many countries now have safeguarding rules, apologies, and in some places payments to survivors. Survivors who speak out say what they need is simpler: to be believed, for the truth to be told, and for it to stop.

If this is your story, simply breathe, and know you can talk to someone you trust or a support line whenever you choose. If it isn't, bring survivors of abuse to mind, in churches and anywhere else, not what happened but them now: getting through a day, being listened to. If you pray, pray for survivors and for leaders to tell the truth; if not, stay with them in silence a while.
Millstone. The weight Jesus says belongs around the neck of anyone who harms a child, a warning answered first by believing survivors.
Your line: believe them. To be believed, and listened to all the way through. That's day nine hundred seventy-four.

975.title: Pentecostalism worldwide
975.hook: from a plain mission on Azusa Street to Pentecostal churches across Africa, Asia and Latin America
975.howItsDone: Pentecostal worship is often loud and expressive, with long sung praise, raised hands, spontaneous prayer, prayer for healing, and speaking in tongues. Charismatic groups in Catholic and other churches pray in similar ways within their own traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: millstone, a wound inside the house, and the millstone Jesus spoke of. Your line: believe them.

No stained glass. No steeple. No pews. On Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a plain wooden building, once used as a stable and a storeroom, has sawdust on the floor and planks laid across barrels for benches. At the front stands a preacher named William Seymour, the son of formerly enslaved parents, with a pair of wooden crates for a pulpit. In the room, Black and white and Latino worshipers, washerwomen and businessmen, side by side, in a city and a country that kept them apart. People pray out loud, weep, sing, and some speak in tongues.

Pentecostalism takes its name from Pentecost, the day in Acts when the Holy Spirit comes on Jesus's followers in Jerusalem. In the King James Bible: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Then Peter stands up and quotes the prophet Joel: "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Pentecostals read that as a promise for now, not only for then. Speaking in tongues, prophecy, prayer for healing: the gifts of the Spirit, they say, are for ordinary believers today. And it showed in who led. At Azusa Street, women preached, and Black and white Christians laid hands on one another, which shocked plenty of observers. One early participant wrote, in effect, that the color line had been washed away. It didn't stay washed; Pentecostal churches later split along racial lines too, and that's part of the story. Some historians say the movement didn't spread from one center like spokes from a hub. They point to revivals with similar marks around the same era in India, Korea, Chile and parts of Africa, many led by local preachers rather than visiting missionaries. Today Pentecostal and charismatic churches are found from Lagos to Seoul to São Paulo, and charismatic renewal has reached Catholic and older Protestant churches too. Christians differ here. Pentecostals say the gifts continue. Some other Christians hold that certain gifts, like tongues, belonged to the apostles' time. Both read the same chapter of Acts.

Bring to mind a Pentecostal or charismatic church you've passed: a rented room above a shop, a big hall by the highway, a congregation meeting in a school gym on Sundays. Picture the people walking in, the music starting, someone raising their hands, and let yourself be curious rather than wary. If you pray, pray for that congregation.
Pentecostalism worldwide. A movement that reads Pentecost as a promise for today, with gifts of the Spirit for ordinary believers, now found across Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Your line: the spirit on all flesh. Sons and daughters alike. Nine hundred seventy-five days now.

976.title: The African church
976.hook: from an Ethiopian official on a desert road to packed churches across the continent, the map of Christianity has shifted south
976.howItsDone: African churches range from the ancient Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo and Coptic Orthodox churches to Catholic, Anglican, Protestant, Pentecostal and African independent churches. Worship is commonly in local languages, with music, singing and dancing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pentecostalism worldwide, and a sawdust floor on Azusa Street. Your line: the spirit on all flesh.

A chariot is rolling along the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem toward Gaza. In it sits a royal treasurer from the court of the queen of the Ethiopians, heading home after worshiping in Jerusalem. A scroll of Isaiah is open on his knees, and he's reading aloud. A man named Philip runs up alongside and calls out, in the King James Bible: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The official invites him up. Further on, they pass some water, and the official says: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" The African church starts earlier than some people expect.

That Ethiopian official goes home baptized, in the eighth chapter of Acts, and the Bible never mentions him again. But Africa doesn't leave the story. Egypt's Coptic Christians trace their church, by tradition, to Mark, the Gospel writer. Some early Christian writers came from North Africa, Augustine among them. Ethiopia has its own ancient church, with scriptures in the old language Ge'ez and churches carved straight down into the rock. So when people call Christianity a Western religion that arrived in Africa with Europeans, the Bible itself and these old churches answer back. Then came a harder chapter. European missionaries arrived alongside colonial rule, and the two got tangled; schools, hospitals and translated Bibles came with land taken and cultures dismissed. Historians of African Christianity also stress that much of the spreading was done by Africans themselves, catechists, evangelists, prophets and ordinary converts, often far beyond any missionary's reach. Some started churches of their own, African independent churches, praying in their own languages and music. Today the continent is full of church life: Anglicans in Nigeria and Uganda, Catholics in Congo, Orthodox in Ethiopia, Pentecostals in Ghana and Kenya, and many more. Some who study world Christianity say its center of gravity has moved south, away from Europe and North America. And traffic now runs both ways: some African churches plant congregations in London, Houston and Berlin. Some readers see the treasurer on the desert road as an early sign of where the story was heading.

Travel the continent in thought: a Coptic church in Cairo, a stone church in the Ethiopian highlands, a cathedral in Kampala, a big Pentecostal gathering in Lagos, then any African congregation meeting in your own city. Stop at one and listen: a choir, a drum, a language you may not know. If you pray, pray for that church and its people; if you don't, send them good will in the quiet.
Ethiopian. The queen's treasurer who read Isaiah on the desert road and was baptized, an early sign some see of the African church to come.
Your line: the center has moved. Africa never left the story, from a desert road to today. Until tomorrow.

977.title: Korean prayer mountains
977.hook: Korean Christians rise before dawn for prayer meetings
977.howItsDone: In South Korea, some Protestant churches hold prayer meetings before dawn on weekdays, where the congregation may pray aloud together, and prayer retreats on hillsides let people go away to pray for a night or longer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ethiopian: a treasurer baptized on a desert road, and churches across a continent. Your line was the center has moved.

It's still dark outside, and the church lights are already on. In South Korea, some congregations meet for prayer before dawn on ordinary weekdays, before the subway fills and the offices open. People come in work clothes. Some kneel, some sit. Then the whole room prays out loud at once, each person in their own words, a sound like rain on a roof. Out on the hillsides there are places set apart only for prayer: prayer mountains, with small rooms and little caves where someone can pray through a night, or a week.

In Korean, the early meeting is called saebyeok gido, dawn prayer. There's a verse that fits the habit. In Mark's Gospel, the whole town had crowded Jesus's door the night before. Then, in the King James Bible: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Mark doesn't say what he prayed. Only when and where: before day, and alone. A few lines later the disciples find him and say, "All men seek for thee." The prayer sits in the gap between last night's crowd and this morning's. A psalm says it from the other side: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." Some readers hear a watchman on a wall, waiting for the light. Now put the two Korean habits beside Mark's verse. The prayer mountain gives his solitary place an address: people climb, sometimes fasting, pray in a small room cut into the hill, and come back down to their lives. The dawn meeting gives his early hour company. Alone on a hill, and together in the dark. Not every Korean church keeps the dawn hour, and Christians pray at other hours too. But the habit has a simple logic: before the phone and the news and the list, the first words of the day can go somewhere else.
screen: `IN THE MORNING, AND WILL LOOK UP.`
`ALONE ON A HILL, TOGETHER IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Whatever the hour where you are, go back to the first minute of today: what got there first, a worry, a screen, someone else's voice? Don't scold yourself; just notice, and give the next two minutes the job the morning might have had. If you pray, borrow the psalm, in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee; if not, face a window, look up, and wait the way a watchman waits for light.
Saebyeok gido. Korean for dawn prayer, prayer that gets there before the day does, kept on hillsides and in city churches before sunrise.
Your line: dawn prayer. The hour before the sun belongs to no one else yet. See you tomorrow.

978.title: China's churches
978.hook: registered and house churches, growing through persecution
978.howItsDone: Some Christians elsewhere pray for the church in China in their own prayers and in services; in China, registered congregations meet in church buildings, while house churches gather in homes and other private spaces.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saebyeok gido, a room praying aloud before sunrise, and your line was dawn prayer.

Two Sunday mornings in the same Chinese city. In the first, a church with its name on the gate: doors open, choir robed, hymn numbers on a board at the front, registered with the state. In the second, an apartment a few streets away. Curtains drawn. Folding chairs borrowed from neighbors who don't ask questions. Someone keeps the singing soft. Both rooms are reading the same Gospel. Both are being watched, in different ways.
screen: `A CHURCH WITH ITS NAME ON THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Christians in China gather in roughly two ways. Registered churches belong to bodies the government recognizes, and meet openly under state rules about what can be taught and who can attend. House churches meet outside that system, in homes, offices, rented rooms. The line between them isn't always neat, and Christians in China disagree about it honestly. Some register so they can worship in the open and serve within the law. Others refuse, because they won't let the state decide what happens in worship. Reports from China describe hard seasons for both: crosses taken down from church roofs, gatherings closed, pastors detained. And still the people keep meeting. Nobody can count them exactly; a church in a living room keeps no public list. Jesus talked about growth you can't watch. In John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." A corn of wheat is just a grain. It goes under before anything comes up. And in Mark, a man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and wakes: "the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how." The farmer isn't in charge of it. An old saying, traced to an early Christian writer named Tertullian, says the blood of Christians is seed. Christians in China wouldn't all put it that way, and the old line is no reason to romanticize suffering. Some readers hear the same picture in what Jesus said: under the ground is not the same as gone.
screen: `A CORN OF WHEAT FALLS INTO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Picture the two rooms from the start, and someone in each: an older woman with a worn Bible, a young man keeping one eye on the door. You don't know their names; hold them anyway. If you pray, pray for Christians in China in both kinds of room, in whatever words you have; if not, simply wish them safety and courage.
China's churches. Registered churches meeting in the open, and house churches meeting outside registration: two ways of gathering, under pressure, around the same Gospel.
Your line: the seed underground. Some growing happens where no one can watch it. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

979.title: Latin America
979.hook: base communities reading the Bible together, and a Pentecostal wave
979.carry: the bible read by the poor
979.howItsDone: Small Bible-sharing groups meet in homes and parishes across Latin America, reading a passage aloud and talking about what it says to their own lives, while Pentecostal congregations gather for lively worship, preaching and prayer for healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, China's churches, one with its name on the gate and one with the curtains drawn, and your line was the seed underground.

A village chapel with a tin roof. The Gospel has just been read: Jesus feeding a hungry crowd. Instead of a sermon, a question goes around the benches. What do you hear? A fisherman says the crowd was hungry because somebody kept the bread. A grandmother says the disciples wanted to send people away, and Jesus said no, you feed them. A teenager asks why their own village is still hungry. Nobody in the room has studied theology. Everybody in the room knows hunger.
screen: `A TIN ROOF, A GOSPEL, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: They were called base communities: small groups of poor Catholics, often led by lay people rather than priests, reading the Bible against their own lives. In Nicaragua, a priest named Ernesto Cardenal wrote down the conversations of the farmers and fishermen in his island parish, and the book became The Gospel in Solentiname. One passage from Luke sounds different in rooms like those. Jesus stands up in the synagogue in his hometown, is handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, and reads, in the King James Bible: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." In a tin-roofed chapel, that line doesn't sound like a metaphor. Alongside these groups grew what was called liberation theology, which spoke of God's special care for the poor. It stirred real argument. Supporters said it was simply the Gospel read honestly from the bottom. Some Catholic leaders, Rome among them, warned against borrowing ideas from Marxism, and the debate was carried on inside the church. Meanwhile a second wave rose in the same neighborhoods: Pentecostal churches, small congregations in rented rooms with guitars, healing prayer and preachers from the block. The two looked nothing alike, and didn't always get along. But both put the Bible in ordinary hands and asked what it said to people who had very little. In Matthew, Jesus says it in a prayer: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes."
screen: `BASE COMMUNITIES: THE BIBLE ON THE BENCHES.`
`A PENTECOSTAL WAVE ON THE SAME BLOCK.`

segments.voice: Say the line from Luke slowly, twice: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor. Then ask the benches' question, what do I hear, not as a scholar would, but about your own street and your own week, and let one honest answer come. If you pray, you can pray the line back.
Latin America. Base communities reading scripture together in small, poor parishes, and a Pentecostal wave in the same streets: the Bible in ordinary hands.
Your line: the bible read by the poor. Nobody on those benches needed a degree to hear it. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine, done.

980.title: Christians of the Middle East
980.hook: the oldest churches, now shrinking; Coptic workers killed in Libya for their faith
980.howItsDone: The ancient churches of the Middle East celebrate long liturgies in Coptic, Syriac, Arabic and Armenian, and some Christians elsewhere pray for them by name in Sunday prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Latin America, a Gospel passed around the benches of a tin-roofed chapel, and your line was the bible read by the poor.

"And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch." That's a line from the book of Acts, and Antioch was a real city in what is now southern Turkey, near the Syrian border. So the name itself was first spoken in the Middle East. This week traveled the map, to Africa, to Korea, to China, to Latin America. It ends where the story began, with churches that were never brought in from somewhere else, because they were there from the start.

In the early chapters of Acts, followers of Jesus are already in Jerusalem, Damascus and Antioch, long before Paul reaches Rome. Churches in those lands still trace themselves to that beginning: the Coptic church in Egypt, the Syriac churches, the Assyrian and Chaldean churches of Iraq, the Maronites of Lebanon, the Armenians. Some still pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Aramaic is the language Mark preserves when Jesus takes a dead girl by the hand. In the King James Bible: "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Mark kept the sound of his words, and these churches keep that family of words in their worship. They aren't a foreign import. They are what was there first. And in place after place they are fewer than their grandparents knew. War, pressure and poverty have pushed families to leave, and some villages that once filled a church now have few Christian households left. Some have stayed at great cost. In Libya, a group of Coptic Christian workers, with a man from Ghana among them, were seized by an extremist group and killed for being Christians. Their killers' video was meant to frighten. Others who watched noticed something else: men on a beach, some praying the name of Jesus as they died. The Coptic Orthodox Church counts them as martyrs, and some of their families said publicly that they forgave. The oldest churches have carried this a long time, and they are still praying in the old words.
screen: `THE MARTYRS ON THE BEACH IN LIBYA.`

segments.voice: Picture three places: a crowded church in Cairo with incense in the air, a village church on the plain near Mosul that families are coming home to repair, a stone chapel in Syria with Aramaic words carved over the door. If you pray, pray for Christians in Egypt, Iraq and Syria, and for everyone in those countries who longs for peace; if not, hold each place with good will; people there are praying this hour too.
Antioch. The city in the Middle East where the name Christian was first used, home to churches that still pray in a form of the language Jesus spoke.
Your line: the oldest churches. A week around the world ends at the beginning. Day nine hundred eighty.
